question: Which writer owns creation of session-state.json, given that ai_router/session_state.py and the extension's utils/sessionState.ts both create it and the extension's copy is reached from a READ (readStatus)?
decision: The router's sanctioned writers own creation. The extension's read path stops writing: readStatus derives the same shape in memory (inferStateInMemory) and readSessionSets uses that derivation when the file is absent. ensureSessionStateFile is removed from the extension; synthesizeNotStartedState survives as an explicit-action writer only, and cancel/restore keep their own sanctioned writer. The rule: the extension writes session-state.json only on an explicit operator action, never on a read. Reversible cheaply — the removed write is one function and its call site, and the in-memory builder is the same code path the writer used.

options.option: Keep both writers and mirror the title logic, enforced by a parity test
options.consequence: The race survives: whichever writer reaches disk first still decides the ledger, and the next field added to the payload re-opens the same defect. Parity would prove agreement about titles, not about who writes.

options.option: Router owns creation; the extension's read derives in memory (chosen)
options.consequence: The race cannot happen — a scan produces no file at all. Removes a writer and an untracked-file side effect Set 099 S2 had already worked around with rawSessionSetStatus. Costs an in-memory branch in readSessionSets so spec-only sets keep their planned rows, and changes three tests that pinned the write side effect.

options.option: Extension owns creation; strip the Python lazy-synth
options.consequence: Inverts the constitution's state-mutation discipline (start_session / close_session are the sanctioned writers) and would leave consumer repos without a state file whenever the Explorer is not open.

question: A generic `Session N` title is sticky because title resolution puts the stored ledger first. 130 rows across the repo carry one, and most belong to CLOSED sets that will never get another boundary write. Where does the heal go, given spec decision 4 says this set does not move title resolution onto the read path?
decision: Heal in BOTH places through one shared pure rule (progress.heal_title, mirrored in progress.ts). The writer heals at every boundary write so the fix persists; the reader heals the display so closed sets — which get no further write — stop lying, with no migration script rewriting closed history. The reader's spec read is CONDITIONAL on needs_title_heal, so a healthy set costs no additional disk read, which is the measured constraint decision 4 was protecting. Reversible: the read-path heal is one guarded block per language.

options.option: Write-path heal only, honouring decision 4 literally
options.consequence: Fails this session's own Ends-with ('existing sets heal themselves'): ~130 rows in closed sets never get another boundary write and stay generic forever.

options.option: Write-path heal plus a conditional read-path heal (chosen)
options.consequence: Every set displays its real titles immediately, including closed ones. Costs one spec read per DRIFTED set per scan and none for healthy sets; the existing readSessionSets perf gate (p95 < 5000ms) is the falsifier.

options.option: A one-shot migration script that rewrites every drifted state file
options.consequence: Rewrites closed sets' records — the thing this repo treats as history — and the spec explicitly asks for healing WITHOUT a migration script. Also leaves the write-path bug in place for the next set.

question: Does the session-scoped reveal need a NEW command and its own file-opening path, or should it go through the existing `dabblerSessionSets.openSpec`?
decision: One command, two callers. `dabblerSessionSets.openSpec` learned to read a session number off its argument (`kind: "session"`) and to open `spec.md` positioned at that session's `### Session N of M:` block; a set node through the same command still opens at the top, byte-identical to before. The tree-level command `dabblerWorkExplorer.activateSession` exists only to narrow the untrusted node and dispatch — the exact shape `activateSet` already has. The heading scan is BORROWED from `sessionStepModel.scanSessionHeads` (mirror of `spec_admission._SESSION_HEAD_RE`) rather than re-derived, so one regex decides where session 3 begins.

options.option: A parallel `openSessionSpec` command with its own existence check, message wording and file resolution
options.consequence: A second place to answer 'which file is the spec' and a second 'Spec does not exist yet' message to keep in sync; the two drift the first time either changes.

options.option: Teach the existing openSpec to take an optional section (chosen)
options.consequence: One file-resolution path, one message, one heading regex shared with the step parser. Costs a narrowing helper that FAILS CLOSED — anything that is not a session node carrying a positive integer opens at the top.

options.option: Spawn the Python extractor (`verify_session.extract_spec_excerpt`) for the section
options.consequence: Puts a process spawn on a click and makes a display feature fail whenever the interpreter is unresolvable — the coupling Set 114 S3 rejected for the step rows.

question: Step 4 asks whether the plain reveal reads as too unfocused in use — and if it does, a read-only virtual document on a custom scheme is the sanctioned next step. Ship the custom scheme now, or ship the plain reveal and let the set's own UAT answer it?
decision: Ship the plain reveal, and record that the question is ANSWERED BY THE OPERATOR at this set's UAT walk, not by the orchestrator's guess. The reveal is deliberate rather than incidental — `showTextDocument` + `revealRange(AtTop)` puts the session's own heading on the first viewport row (proven in a real host, `session-plan-reveal.spec.ts`), and the selection is left EMPTY so no 40-line highlight is painted over a file the operator is about to read. That is the strongest form of 'the plain reveal' available, so if it still reads as unfocused, the finding is about the FORMAT and not about the implementation. No custom scheme is added on this evidence: the spec's non-goals refuse one 'unless Session 2 measures the plain reveal as insufficient', and nothing measured here is insufficient — the operator lands in the real file, at the real section, with the surrounding context and the configuration block a scroll away, which is exactly what decisions 1-3 bought.

options.option: Ship the plain reveal; the set's UAT walk decides whether it is focused enough (chosen)
options.consequence: Zero new surface, and the question stays open on evidence rather than being closed by a reflex. If the walk says it is unfocused, the custom scheme is a recorded follow-up with a named reason — which is what the spec asks for.

options.option: Add a read-only virtual document on a custom scheme now
options.consequence: A second rendering of the truth on screen, a new scheme to register and keep alive, and the operator loses the surrounding spec context the set explicitly chose to keep. Taken pre-emptively it would be the 'default, not a decision' the spec warns against.

options.option: Select the whole session block instead of placing an empty cursor
options.consequence: More visibly 'focused' for one second, then a large highlight over unread text that the first keystroke would replace. Rejected as a worse default, not deferred.

question: Step 3 says gate the session run prompt on status the way `planLeftClickActivation` does. Taken literally that puts "Copy Run Prompt" on EVERY non-terminal session row. But the framework's only documented run trigger is set-scoped â€” `Start the next session of `<slug>`.` (workflow doc, Trigger Phrases) â€” so on session 4 while session 3 is next, that prompt starts a DIFFERENT session than the row it was copied from. Offer the prompt on every non-terminal session, invent a session-scoped trigger phrase, or gate it to the session the phrase would actually run?
decision: Gate it to the session the phrase actually runs, and copy the documented phrase verbatim. The action's `when` is the conjunction of two existing rules and one new one: the set-level gate is `planLeftClickActivation(set.name, set.state).clipboardWrite !== null` â€” reused, not re-implemented, so the set row and the session row cannot drift on what a runnable set is â€” and the session-level rule is `nextRunnableSessionNumber(sessions)`: walk the ledger in ascending number order, skip `complete` and `cancelled`, and the first survivor is the candidate; it is runnable only if its status is `in-progress` or `not-started`. An unrecognised status therefore yields NO offer anywhere in the set, which is the fail-closed posture step 3 names. The copied text is `buildStartNextSessionPrompt(set)` â€” the same builder the set row's L5 shortcut uses. No new trigger-phrase vocabulary is minted.

options.option: Gate to the next runnable session; copy the documented set-scoped phrase (chosen)
options.consequence: The prompt on a row always starts THAT row's session, because the only row that carries it is the one the phrase resolves to. Costs discoverability: sessions 4..N show no run prompt. That is honest â€” they are not runnable yet, and the workflow is strictly sequential (`start_session` infers max(closed)+1).

options.option: Offer on every non-terminal session, copying the same set-scoped phrase
options.consequence: A lie by placement: pasting the prompt copied from session 4 starts session 3. This is precisely the class of defect the repo's documentation-authority principle exists to prevent, and the operator would only discover it after an orchestrator had already registered the wrong session.

options.option: Mint a session-scoped trigger phrase (`Start session N of `<slug>`.`)
options.consequence: An extension session would be defining a new orchestrator contract that lives in `docs/ai-led-session-workflow.md` and is honoured only by an LLM's goodwill â€” no gate enforces it. It also invites out-of-order starts, which the sequential lifecycle and the close gates assume cannot happen. Rejected as scope expansion, not deferred.

question: Step 4 wants the artifact menu entry to discover files by convention (`s<N>-*`) and to show an honest empty state. Should the entry be HIDDEN on sessions that have produced nothing â€” which would need a directory listing per session row on the tree scan â€” or always shown and answered at click time?
decision: Always show the entry; answer at click time. Hiding it would require reading every set directory during the tree scan to know whether `s<N>-*` exists, which is exactly the per-scan disk read Set 115's decision 4 and Set 110 S1's measured startup budget forbid. The read happens on the CLICK â€” the same seam Session 2 established for the spec read â€” and an empty result is reported as a plain informational message naming the session, the set and the `s<N>-*` convention, so the operator learns the rule from the empty state rather than from the docs. Discovery is `^s<N>-` on the top-level entries of the set directory, case-insensitively, files only, sorted by name: `s3-` cannot collide with `s30-` (the delimiter follows the digits), the prefix is the convention every existing artifact already obeys (`s1-issues.json`, `s2-verification-round-2.md`), and it mirrors the existing `ISSUES_FILE_RE` reader in `utils/fileSystem.ts` rather than inventing a second naming authority. One match opens directly; several open a QuickPick â€” the same shape `openPrerequisiteSpec` already uses.

options.option: Always show; discover and answer at click time (chosen)
options.consequence: No new I/O on any hot path, one code path for every session, and 'nothing yet' is a sentence the operator can act on. The cost is a menu entry that can lead to a message instead of a file.

options.option: Hide the entry when the session has no artifacts
options.consequence: A readdir per session row on every scan and every watcher tick â€” the measured constraint the set spent Session 1 protecting. It also makes 'no artifacts' indistinguishable from 'feature missing', which is a worse answer than the message.

options.option: Enumerate a hardcoded list of known artifact names
options.consequence: Explicitly refused by step 4. The set's own directory carries fourteen distinct `s1-*`/`s2-*` shapes today and gains new ones per set; a list would silently drop whatever a future session invents.
